title: Distributed Transactions
concept: A distributed transaction makes several changes, spread across shards or services, happen all-or-nothing: either every part commits or none does. The strongly consistent way is two-phase commit, where a coordinator first asks every participant to prepare and then, only if all agree, tells them to commit, with each participant's agreement durably replicated by consensus. The looser way is a saga: a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails, which trades the strict guarantee for availability. Either way the hard parts are the same: a round of coordination adds latency, and a failure mid-way must leave the system in a defined state.

points: A distributed transaction makes changes across shards or services happen all-or-nothing: every part commits or none does.
Two-phase commit has a coordinator ask every participant to prepare, then commit only if all agree; a saga chains local transactions with compensating undo steps.
Google's Percolator builds cross-shard transactions on a store with only single-row atomicity, using one designated row's atomic write as the commit point.
Cockroach Labs found transaction latency is dominated by synchronous replication rounds in series, and pipelining overlaps those rounds.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why a change that spans shards needs more than a single-node transaction, and what all-or-nothing means across machines.
why.body:
A single database gives you a transaction for free: begin, make several changes, commit, and either all of them stick or none do. Once the data is sharded across machines, or split across services that each own their own database, that guarantee is gone. Moving money from an account on shard A to one on shard B is two writes on two machines, and if the first commits and the second fails, the money has vanished.

A distributed transaction restores all-or-nothing across those machines. The difficulty is that there is no single place that can flip everything at once: each participant commits locally, and the network between them can drop messages or a participant can crash at the worst moment. So the system needs a protocol that reaches an agreement to commit, records that decision durably so it survives crashes, and defines exactly what happens if a participant disappears half-way. That protocol, and its cost, is what this topic is about.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture a coordinator driving a two-phase commit and see where the decision becomes final.
mentalModel.body:
Picture one coordinator and several participants, each owning a shard; this protocol is two-phase commit, or 2PC. In the first phase, prepare, the coordinator asks every participant "can you commit this, and will you hold it ready?" Each participant does the work tentatively, makes it durable, and replies yes or no. In the second phase, commit, the coordinator looks at the replies: if every participant said yes, it records "commit" and tells them all to finalise; if any said no or went silent, it records "abort" and tells them to roll back.

The single most important point is the commit point: the instant the coordinator durably records the decision. Before it, nothing is final and everyone can still abort. After it, the outcome is fixed, and even if the coordinator crashes, recovery reads that record and drives every participant to the same conclusion. Because each participant's prepared state and the coordinator's decision must survive crashes, they are replicated by consensus, which is why distributed transactions sit on top of the consensus you already learned.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through prepare, the commit point, finalise, and what recovery does after a crash.

steps.step: Begin and do the work tentatively
steps.explanation: The coordinator starts the transaction and sends each participant its part. Each writes the change in a tentative form, often as a lock (a mark that stops others changing the row) plus a pending value, so it is ready to commit but not yet visible.

Each participant makes its tentative state durable, replicated by consensus so it survives a crash, and votes yes only if it can guarantee it will be able to commit. A participant that cannot votes no.

The coordinator collects the votes. If all are yes it durably records commit; if any is no or times out it records abort. This recorded decision is the commit point, the instant the outcome becomes final.

The coordinator tells every participant the decision. On commit they make their tentative value visible and release locks; on abort they discard it. Participants can be told lazily, because the decision is already durable.

If the coordinator crashes, recovery reads the decision record: committed transactions are driven to finalise, undecided ones are aborted. If a participant crashes, it rejoins and asks the coordinator (or the record) what was decided.

When holding locks across a long or cross-service workflow is too costly, a saga runs each step as its own committed local transaction and, on failure, runs compensating transactions in reverse to undo the completed steps, accepting intermediate states in exchange for no held locks. Isolation, meaning that concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work, is weaker as a result.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace a cross-shard transfer through two-phase commit and see what a crash at each stage does.

steps.explanation: Debit account X on shard A by 100, credit account Y on shard B by 100. The two must both happen or neither; a partial result loses or invents money.
The coordinator asks A to prepare the debit and B to prepare the credit. Each checks it can do its part (X has funds; Y exists), writes the change tentatively and durably, and votes yes.
Both voted yes, so the coordinator durably records "commit". This is the commit point: the transfer is now going to happen even if something crashes next.

steps.step: A crash after the commit point
steps.explanation: Suppose the coordinator crashes before telling B to finalise. On recovery it reads "commit" and re-sends the finalise to B. The credit is applied; the transfer completes. Nothing is lost because the decision was durable.

steps.step: A crash before the commit point
steps.explanation: If instead a shard crashed during prepare and could not vote yes, the coordinator records "abort". Both shards discard their tentative changes on recovery, so X keeps its 100 and no partial transfer remains.

Both accounts were locked from prepare until finalise, so other transfers touching X or Y waited. That held-lock window, plus the round trips to prepare and commit, is the price two-phase commit pays for atomicity. Pipelining, issuing writes without waiting for each to replicate and confirming them all at commit, cuts the wait for each write to replicate during the transaction.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid three mistakes with distributed transactions.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: What is the defining guarantee of a distributed transaction across shards?
options: Every shard commits its part all-or-nothing, so there is never a partial result
Each shard commits independently and you hope they agree
Only the first shard's write matters
quiz.why: Atomicity across machines is the whole point: either all participants commit or all abort, so a transfer can never leave money debited but not credited.
wrong: Independent commits with no agreement are exactly the partial-failure problem a distributed transaction exists to prevent.
All participants' writes matter; ignoring the others would drop part of the transaction.

quiz.question: In two-phase commit, what happens during the prepare phase?
options: The coordinator immediately makes all changes visible to readers, then asks whether anyone objects
Participants release their locks and discard their pending work so the coordinator can start cleanly
Each participant durably readies its change and votes yes or no, but nothing is final yet
quiz.why: Prepare makes each participant's change durable and gets its vote, so the coordinator can then decide; nothing commits until the decision is recorded.
wrong: Changes are not made visible in prepare; that happens only after the commit decision.
Prepare keeps the pending change and its locks; discarding them would make a yes vote meaningless.

quiz.question: The coordinator durably records "commit", then crashes before telling one participant. What happens on recovery?
options: The whole transaction is lost, because only the coordinator knew it had ever started
Recovery reads the committed decision and drives that participant to finalise
The participant waits a while and then decides for itself whether to commit or abort
quiz.why: The commit point is the durable decision record, so recovery can always complete a committed transaction and no acknowledged commit is lost.
wrong: A recorded commit is not lost; durability of the decision is what makes 2PC safe across crashes.
A participant follows the recorded coordinator decision rather than deciding alone.

quiz.question: What is the main cost two-phase commit pays for its all-or-nothing guarantee?
options: It can only ever involve one shard
Participants hold locks from prepare until finalise, and coordination adds round trips
quiz.why: Each participant must hold its prepared state locked until it hears the decision, so other work on that data waits, and the prepare and commit rounds add latency.
wrong: 2PC exists precisely to span multiple shards; one shard would not need it.
2PC either commits all the writes or aborts them all, so none are silently dropped.

quiz.question: When is a saga a better fit than two-phase commit?
options: When locks across a long, cross-service workflow cost too much and steps can be compensated
When you need the strictest possible isolation between concurrent transactions in every service
When all the data lives in one database
quiz.why: A saga commits each step locally and undoes with compensations on failure, so it holds no cross-service locks, at the price of visible intermediate states.
wrong: A saga gives up strict isolation; if you need that, 2PC or a single-node transaction fits better.
If all the data is in one database you can use a local transaction and need neither 2PC nor a saga.

quiz.question: Why do distributed transactions build on consensus?
options: Consensus makes the whole transaction run on one machine, so no cross-shard coordination is left
Consensus removes the need for a commit decision, because replicas simply vote on every write
Prepared votes and the commit decision must survive crashes, and consensus makes them durable
quiz.why: A prepared vote and the commit record must not be lost if a node crashes, so they are replicated by consensus, which is why this topic sits on top of consensus.
wrong: Consensus coordinates replicas and leaves the transaction spread across machines.
The commit decision is essential, and consensus is what makes it durable.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how a system builds distributed transactions on a key-value store and how another makes them fast.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can tell apart building atomic transactions on top of simpler storage and optimising their latency on top of consensus.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can pick a transaction strategy for a workflow, design for crash recovery, and reduce cross-shard transaction latency.

exercises.prompt: An order service, a payment service and an inventory service each own their database. A checkout must charge payment, reserve stock, and create the order, all-or-nothing. Would you use two-phase commit or a saga, and why?
exercises.answer: A saga fits better here. These are independent services with their own databases, and a long-held cross-service lock during 2PC would hurt availability and throughput. Model checkout as a saga: create the order (pending), reserve stock, charge payment; if a later step fails, run compensations in reverse (refund, release stock, cancel order). Make each step idempotent (safe to repeat), since steps and compensations may be retried.
exercises.tradeoffs: The saga exposes intermediate states (an order briefly pending, stock briefly reserved) and needs compensations written and tested for every step. In return it holds no cross-service locks and each service stays independent. If strict isolation were required, 2PC or a single owning service would be the alternative.
wrongAnswers: Hold a two-phase-commit lock across all three services for the whole checkout.
Fire the three calls with no coordination and hope they all succeed.
Skip compensations and leave partial state on failure.

exercises.prompt: You are building distributed transactions on a key-value store that only guarantees single-row atomic writes. How do you get all-or-nothing across many rows that may live on different shards?
exercises.answer: Use two-phase commit layered on the single-row primitive, as Google's Percolator does. Give each transaction a designated primary row whose single-row write is the atomic commit point; prewrite each participating row with a lock that points at the primary, then commit by flipping the primary row. A reader that finds a lock looks up the primary to learn whether the transaction committed. Use a timestamp authority and snapshot isolation so reads see a consistent version. The store's single-row atomicity is the foundation the protocol is built from.
exercises.tradeoffs: This adds several extra store operations per logical write (Percolator reports roughly a factor-of-four overhead versus raw Bigtable on its worst-case benchmark, a single-cell write and commit), and latency rises with the number of rows. In return you get cross-row, cross-shard atomicity on storage that never promised it.
wrongAnswers: Assume multi-row atomicity the store does not provide.
Write each row independently with no commit point, risking partial transactions.
Ignore isolation so readers see half-applied transactions.

exercises.prompt: Cross-shard SQL transactions in your database are slow because each statement waits for a full consensus round before the next runs. How do you cut the latency without weakening consistency?
exercises.answer: Pipeline the consensus rounds instead of serialising them, as CockroachDB does. Rather than waiting for each statement's write to be fully replicated before issuing the next, issue the writes and let their consensus rounds proceed concurrently, tracking the outstanding ones, and only wait for all of them to have replicated at commit time. That turns the replication-latency cost from one round per statement (O(n), growing with the number of statements) toward a single wait at the end (O(1) rounds), without changing what is ultimately committed.
exercises.tradeoffs: Pipelining adds bookkeeping to track in-flight writes and to re-drive or abort cleanly if one fails, and the final commit still waits for the slowest outstanding round. It reduces latency, not the total work, and the consistency guarantee is unchanged.
wrongAnswers: Drop below a majority quorum to go faster, breaking consistency.
Keep serialising every statement and just add hardware.
Weaken isolation to skip the coordination entirely.

next.body: Distributed transactions lean directly on Consensus for durable agreement and on Sharding for the data they span, and they inherit the CAP trade-off between staying consistent and staying available. The saga alternative connects back to Message Queues and Event-driven Architecture, where each step and its compensation are messages. Failover keeps the coordinator and participants alive. posts.title: Large-scale Incremental Processing Using Distributed Transactions and Notifications
posts.ageNote: This is a research paper, not a company blog post: the 2010 OSDI Percolator paper. It is here for a fundamental that has not changed: how to build cross-row, cross-shard two-phase-commit transactions on top of a store that only offers single-row atomicity, using a primary lock as the commit point and snapshot isolation. Google's indexing systems have evolved since, so treat the figures as of 2010 and the mechanism as the lasting lesson.

digest.problem: Google needed to update its web index incrementally as each new page was crawled, instead of rebuilding the whole index in big batches. Doing that means many small, concurrent updates that must stay consistent, but the underlying store, Bigtable, only guaranteed atomic writes to a single row. Percolator adds ACID, cross-row, cross-shard transactions on top of that single-row primitive so incremental indexing stays correct.
digest.constraints: The system runs across thousands of unreliable machines, so a transaction must survive crashes and partitions. It must provide snapshot isolation so concurrent transactions see a consistent version of the data, and it is built strictly on top of the single-row transactions Bigtable already provides, with no new storage layer.

walkthrough.explanation: Percolator takes Bigtable's one guarantee, atomic single-row writes, as its foundation and composes a multi-row, multi-shard transaction protocol from it using two-phase commit.
A central timestamp service hands out strictly increasing timestamps, which Percolator uses to implement snapshot isolation: each transaction reads at one timestamp and commits at a later one.
In the first phase the transaction writes each participating cell tentatively and places a lock on it. One of the locks is designated the primary; all the others point at it.

The commit point is a single-row write that clears the primary lock and records the commit timestamp. Because that one write is atomic in Bigtable, the whole transaction becomes committed at that instant.
A reader that encounters a lock follows it to the primary to learn whether the transaction committed, then cleans up or waits accordingly, so no coordinator is needed on the read path.
Observers watch for changed cells and run follow-on transactions, which is how one crawled document incrementally updates everything that depends on it.

tradeoffs.chosen: Two-phase commit with a primary-lock commit point and snapshot isolation, layered on Bigtable's single-row writes, to get cross-shard ACID transactions for incremental indexing.
tradeoffs.rejected: The previous MapReduce approach, which had to be re-run over the entire repository, old pages and new.
tradeoffs.why: Incremental indexing needs many small consistent updates, which MapReduce cannot process individually because it relies on large batches. Google accepted roughly a fourfold overhead on its worst-case benchmark, and higher latency, in exchange for cutting the average age of documents in search results by 50% for the same number of documents per day, with much smoother resource usage.

digest.failures: The paper is honest that transactions are not free: Percolator incurs roughly four times the overhead of raw Bigtable when writing a single cell and committing, which the paper calls its worst case, and workers batch their timestamp requests to the oracle to save RPC overhead at the cost of higher transaction latency. It also depends on a central timestamp oracle, which the paper says serves around 2 million timestamps per second from a single machine, and on correct lock cleanup when transactions or readers crash.
digest.takeaways: You can build strong, cross-shard transactions on top of a store that only promises single-row atomicity, by using one designated row's atomic write as the commit point and timestamps for isolation. The durable lesson is the shape of two-phase commit and the idea of a single atomic commit point, plus the honest reminder that this atomicity is bought with real per-operation overhead.

posts.title: How Pipelining consensus writes speeds up distributed SQL transactions
posts.ageNote: From January 2019, included for a fundamental that has not changed: distributed transaction latency on a consensus-replicated store is dominated by the number of synchronous consensus rounds, and pipelining those rounds reduces it. CockroachDB has added further optimisations since (such as parallel commits), so treat the specifics as the 2019 state and the latency model as the lasting lesson.

digest.problem: CockroachDB supports ACID transactions across arbitrary data in a distributed SQL database, but it had to pay for that consistency in transaction latency. Compared with consensus systems offering weaker transaction semantics, it often performed more synchronous consensus rounds to run a transaction, so a multi-statement transaction's latency grew with the number of statements.
digest.constraints: The database keeps strong consistency and uses the Raft consensus protocol to coordinate replicas and achieve fault tolerance, so each write's durability costs a replication round. Because linearizable ordering does not hold across Ranges, it needs a distributed transaction protocol, one inspired in part by Google Percolator, that breaks a transaction into distinct phases.

walkthrough.step: See where the latency comes from
walkthrough.explanation: A transaction's cost is modelled as storage latency (writing durably) plus replication latency (the Raft round to replicate each write to a majority). The replication rounds dominate multi-statement transactions.
Originally each statement's write waited for its consensus round to finish before the next statement ran, so n statements meant n sequential replication rounds: an O(n) latency cost.

The optimisation introduces concurrency between the rounds: the transaction issues each write and lets its Raft replication proceed in the background, tracking the outstanding ones instead of blocking on each.

Before committing, the transaction waits for all the outstanding replication rounds to have succeeded. The waits overlap, so the many rounds collapse toward a single wait at the end: an O(1) cost in consensus rounds.

Pipelining changes when the system waits for replication, not what it commits. Statements that touch the same rows get a pipeline dependency, so a later one waits for the earlier one's write to be proven; this pipeline stall keeps read-your-writes correct.

In the TPC-C New-Order experiment, each extra millisecond of inter-node latency added 6 ms of transaction latency without pipelining and 2 ms with it

tradeoffs.chosen: Pipeline the per-statement consensus rounds so they run concurrently and are proven once at commit, reducing latency from O(n) to O(1) rounds while keeping ACID.
tradeoffs.rejected: Parallel statement execution (clients add RETURNING NOTHING and get a fake result) and buffering all writes until commit (large buffers, size limits, more aborts at serializable isolation).
tradeoffs.why: The post says the buffering prototype caused a large uptick in transaction aborts under TPC-C at serializable isolation, and writing intents early is what sequences conflicting transactions. Pipelining keeps eager intent writes and starts consensus for them without waiting, then proves them all before commit, so the post reports the latency model matched its experiments.

digest.failures: The post describes earlier failures and its own limits. Parallel statement execution, from v1.0, made clients add RETURNING NOTHING and returned a fake result, so the real row count was lost and a failed write's error arrived later in the transaction. A prototype that buffered all writes until commit was rejected: it needed large buffers on the coordinator and size limits, and it caused more aborts at serializable isolation. Pipelining still has limits: statements touching the same rows cause a pipeline stall, and in the worst case latency returns to the serial model. Each extra statement still cost a little under half a millisecond in its experiment, and commit still takes two consensus rounds, so parallel commits is previewed to cut that to one.
digest.takeaways: On a consensus-replicated store, distributed transaction latency is dominated by how many synchronous replication rounds you force in series. Pipelining them, so they overlap and are confirmed once at commit, turns an O(n) cost into O(1) rounds with the same guarantees, a reminder that you often buy performance by removing coordination from the critical path rather than by weakening correctness.

comparison:
Both posts are about ACID transactions across a distributed store, and both build on simpler guarantees underneath, but one is about making such transactions exist and the other about making them fast, so they read naturally as mechanism then optimisation. Percolator shows how to construct two-phase-commit transactions on a store that only promises single-row atomicity; CockroachDB's pipelining post assumes that kind of protocol and attacks its latency. In fact CockroachDB says its distributed transaction protocol was inspired in part by Percolator, so the second post is in a direct line from the first.

Where they diverge is the problem each solves. Percolator's challenge is correctness without a transactional store: it invents a primary-lock commit point and uses a timestamp oracle for snapshot isolation, accepting a large per-operation overhead to get cross-shard atomicity at all. CockroachDB's challenge is latency given a transactional, consensus-replicated store: it keeps the guarantees but overlaps the consensus rounds that dominate a multi-statement transaction, turning them from serial to pipelined.

The evidence matches that split. Percolator's numbers are about cost paid for atomicity, roughly a fourfold overhead versus raw Bigtable on single-cell writes, across thousands of machines, in service of fresher incremental indexes. CockroachDB's number is about latency removed, from O(n) consensus rounds down to O(1) by pipelining, with the committed result unchanged. Together they show distributed transactions as a layered idea: first a protocol that gives you all-or-nothing across shards, then the engineering that keeps its latency bearable.

glossary.definition: A chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails.
An action that semantically undoes a committed step of a saga, such as a refund for a charge.
Letting several consensus rounds run concurrently and confirming them once at commit, cutting latency.

mistakes: Doing the writes to each shard independently and hoping they all succeed. Without a commit protocol, a crash between writes leaves a partial result, which is exactly the lost-or-invented-money problem distributed transactions prevent.

Forgetting the commit point and crash recovery. Two-phase commit is only safe because the decision is durably recorded before participants finalise; if you make changes visible before recording the decision, a crash can leave shards disagreeing.

Reaching for two-phase commit for every cross-service workflow. Holding locks across services for a long operation hurts availability; when intermediate states can be compensated, a saga is often the better fit, at the cost of strict isolation.
